title: The Windows registry and configuration files on Linux

videos.script: Every setting a program remembers has to be written somewhere. The printer the accounting program uses, the server a backup copies to, how long the system keeps its logs. When something stops working after a change, the question is where that change was written, and whether it can be put back. {{where}} Linux answers with text files, most of them in one folder, slash etc. You can read them with cat, compare them with diff, and copy them before touching them. Windows answers with the registry, one large tree that every program shares and that only special tools open. The Mac uses both, in its own way. {{answers}} Neither is better. Text files are transparent and scattered; the registry is uniform and opaque. What matters is knowing where to look, and how to change a setting so that the change can be undone. {{undo}} In this lesson you will look around slash etc, and read a configuration file that is mostly comments. You will change one safely and put it back, and find each person's own settings in their home folder. Then the registry: its hives, keys and values, how to read and change them, and how to back them up first. {{steps}} The Linux transcripts come from lesson 3's server. The registry and the Mac commands are shown, not run. {{honest}}
